subject: fennec
pitch: A fennec fox kit standing alert on a little sand dune at dusk. Enormous satin ears lined in pale peach, cream fur warming to sandy gold along its back, a fluffy tail with a smudge of black at the tip, and big dark eyes with a tiny white sparkle. Its paws are a touch oversized, like it hasn't grown into them yet, and it wears a woven leather collar with a small brass bell.
reasoning:
I'm mapping out the SDK's API surface—builder creation, joint definitions with positioning and orientation, and the overall structure I'll need to construct a working TypeScript module.

There are also various curve helpers like bezier, catmull, arc, and spiral for generating paths. I'm noting a naming conflict between `mix` exported from paint and the weight-mixing `mix` from context — since explicit named exports override star exports, paint's `mix` wins, though it doesn't really matter here.

For materials, colour strings use a matte material while paint-based fills use a shared sheet, so I should lean on paint functions like gradients or banded colors for details like a tail-tip smudge. For the eyes, I'm thinking simple dark spheres with a tiny offset white sphere for the sparkle highlight, and for the ears I'm planning extruded triangular shapes lined in pale peach.

For the ear lining specifically, I'm weighing whether to use a normal-based paint function versus just layering two extrudes -- an outer darker shell and a smaller peach-colored inner piece offset slightly forward -- which feels simpler and more reliable than testing surface normals. Now I'm moving on to the overall scale of the fox, thinking through realistic proportions for a fennec kit around shoulder height.

I'm setting up the coordinate convention with Y up, Z forward, and considering how to handle the ground: whether the dune the fox stands on should be part of the model itself so the lowest point still touches y=0, with the fox's feet resting higher on top of the sand mound.

I'm sketching out how to shape that dune as scenery—thinking through a lathe-based dome versus an extruded ridge profile to give it a more natural, asymmetric dune silhouette rather than a simple symmetric bump.

I'm sketching a dune profile that tapers down to a point and closes along the axis, with the closing edge collapsing to a zero-width segment at x=0 — degenerate triangles that should render fine but are worth double-checking for safety.

As an alternative, I'm considering building the dune from a scaled hemisphere sphere geometry instead, attaching it as a part to some joint — maybe the root or a dedicated "ground" joint — since parts need a bone reference even if the dune itself doesn't need rigging.

Thinking further, I decide against a standalone ground joint and instead attach the dune part to the hips joint, since the skeleton should have one clear root and the rig constraint matters more for creature anatomy than for scenery. Now I'm turning to how to structure the overall SDK code carefully, since there's a lot of it and I need to get the call signatures right to avoid runtime errors.

I start working through the fox skeleton design: a small alert kit standing on a dune, facing +Z, with proportions and joint positions needing to be worked out so feet rest naturally at the sand's surface. I'm calculating the dune's height profile and how the fox's feet should sink slightly into the crest, checking the surface height at the fox's foot radius to make sure the stance looks grounded rather than floating.

I'll go with the dune, painting it with a warm gold-to-mauve gradient to suggest dusk lighting. Now I'm sketching the fennec kit's proportions: shoulder height around 0.2m, oversized ears about 0.13m tall, body sitting atop the dune at y≈0.10, with a skeleton defining hips, spine curve, and relatively long legs (~0.17m) descending from hip to paw to match the fennec's leggy build.

Front legs go shoulder at y=0.27 down to elbow at 0.18 and foot at 0.10, while back legs run hip at 0.27 through knee at 0.20, hock at 0.13, to paw at 0.10. I'm working out how to rig these using polyline chains, where each span creates a joint, so I need to carefully name joints like shoulder/elbow/wrist per leg to keep the puppet's bone hierarchy clean.

For the actual geometry, sweeping the leg chain gives smooth tubes, and I'm planning to add oversized paws using a sphere primitive scaled non-uniformly along each axis to flatten it into a paw shape, attached to the wrist/ankle bone. I'm confirming that non-uniform scale will bake correctly into world space when the mesh gets painted, since the transform composition should handle it fine as long as there's no skew.

For the head, I'm thinking of using a loft through several stations along the snout-to-skull axis, varying width and height to get a stylized fox wedge shape, rigidly attached to a head joint with its own orientation aimed along the snout.

Checking on how color and bone weighting work in the sweep/loft options -- color seems required, and if I pass an explicit bone like the head joint, the whole loft should skin rigidly to it with uniform weights, which is exactly what I want for a solid head shape.

Now I'm planning the scene components one by one, starting with the dune as background scenery using a lathe revolve with a sand-to-mauve gradient, making sure the `at` position and `bone` binding are set explicitly so it doesn't accidentally rig to the wrong nearby joint once the skeleton exists.

I'm deciding to put a dedicated "hips" joint as the body's root and attach the dune lathe to that bone rather than trying to inject a raw three.js mesh directly into the root group, since the SDK's part functions expect joint ownership and this keeps everything consistent with how posing will move the scenery.

For the torso, I'm weighing a chain-and-sweep approach against a station-based loft — using a spine chain with hips, waist, and chest joints and a radius function that varies width and height along t, versus defining explicit stations with full widths/heights and letting the loft catmull-interpolate the sweep path while still binding to the spine chain as the bone reference.

I'm leaning toward chains for bending body parts and rigid lofts for the head, and now thinking through how a three-point spine path naming its joints affects parent-child relationships in the rig, with the root "hips" joint parenting the chain's first generated joint.

For practical construction, I'll use explicit `b.joint` calls for named joints that need precise orientation, and reserve `b.chain` for limbs where bending matters—then feed those joints into `sweep` via its `bone` option so the mesh skins smoothly along the skeleton using closest-point projection and blended joint spans.

For ears, I'm planning flat extruded leaf shapes rooted at head joints, with inner peach-colored faces and darker sand-toned outer faces determined by normal direction relative to the head.

Since fennec ears rotate forward, the inside of the ear faces front, so I'll make that the peach-lined face and the back dark sand, using the surface normal's z-component to decide which color applies to each side of the extruded shape.

The ear's actual silhouette needs sizing: on a 0.2m head, these oversized fennec ears should be roughly 0.13m tall and about 0.09m wide at the base, shaped like a rounded triangle with a smooth tip rather than sharp corners.

I'll taper the extrusion thickness so the ear is thicker at the base and thinner toward the tip, and add a slight bevel for softer rounded rims.

For orientation, I need to figure out how to place each ear's extrusion plane so the ears tilt outward and slightly forward/back relative to the head, defining the x and y basis vectors per ear side and computing the resulting face normal from their cross product.

Then for shading, I'm deciding how to paint the ear surfaces based on which face is visible: the front-facing side (toward +Z) gets the peach inner lining color, while the back gets the darker sand tone, with the rim edges needing their own blending rule since their normals sit in-plane rather than pointing clearly front or back.

I'll do a simpler gradient instead: front face shifts from cream-tan at the base to peach near the tip, using the surface coordinate passed into the paint function when the part is extruded. For the ear's finer character, I'm considering whether fennec ear tips have any darker marking, though I might skip extra fur details for simplicity.

Now I'm working out body proportions for the loft-based head and torso. I'm sketching joint positions for hips, shoulders, neck base, and head center, aiming for an alert kit pose with the head raised and snout pointed slightly upward, while cross-checking against realistic fox kit proportions for body length, neck, head, and ear size.

I'm reconsidering the overall scale since initial estimates made the figure too tall and too long nose-to-tail compared to a real fennec kit, so I'm compressing the torso, legs, and head lengths and resetting target coordinates: dune/ground level, feet position, shoulder height, head top, and ear tip height, along with snout and tail tip z-positions to keep the final figure around a believable 0.35–0.45 m scale.

Now I'm sketching the dune's lathe profile, plotting radius-height coordinate pairs to shape a gently sloped mound with a flattened crest, while placing the fox's paws near the center where the surface height is around 0.065, and considering a smoothing parameter for the lathe geometry.

I'm also weighing whether a simpler scaled sphere hemisphere would be more robust than the lathe approach, but decide to stick with the lathe since it gives finer control over the dune's actual shape despite the edge-case corner smoothing on the axis.

The lathe profile's closed outline should be valid since adjacent points sharing an axis corner don't count as crossings, and the segments setting with default smoothing should look fine. I also realize the bottom edge of the profile (running along y=0) naturally produces a flat disc at the base, which keeps the mesh watertight and sitting flush on the floor — a minor, mostly invisible detail. Now I'm thinking about shading the dune with a warm sand gradient toward the top.

I want the dune's coloring to shift between a warm gold sand at the top and a dusky mauve along the sides, using a countershading function with a mottled sand texture layered underneath for grain. Combining mottle and countershade should give a dusk-toned, slightly textured look where the top stays golden and the sides fade into purple-mauve as the surface normal tilts outward. I'll skip adding ripple detail for now and move on to the body.

Now I'm working out the skeleton stations for the fox kit's torso and head — placing hips, waist, chest, shoulders, neck base, and head joints at specific heights and depths to establish a slim, alert-posture body, then positioning the skull and snout tip so the head tilts up and forward, while sorting out whether the head loft points should be computed in world space or joint-local space.

Next I'm defining the head profile as a series of width/height stations running from the back of the skull through the cheeks, muzzle, and nose tip, sized so the catmull spline produces a rounded cap at the nose. I'm also noting I'll need fennec-style cream cheek/muzzle markings and a dark nose tip, possibly adding cheek fluff via extra geometry later.

For the eyes, I'm planning to seat them using surface hit detection on the head mesh, finding the nearest point and normal so the eye sticks outward correctly with proper embedding, then placing a small white sparkle sphere slightly offset on the eye's front-upper surface using a local frame transform.

So the eye embeds about 0.6r into the skull with roughly 0.4r bulging outward, which fits the fennec's big-eyed look — I'll use embed 0.4 with radius 0.018 for the right proportions. For the sparkle highlight, I'm positioning a tiny white sphere slightly outside the eye's surface, offset upward and forward from the eye's center along its outward normal and local up/forward axes.

For attaching the eye to the skull surface, I'm pulling the nearest point and normal off the head loft mesh using a surface query, then sticking the eye sphere there with rigid binding to the head joint. The eye part returned from the stick call gives me its origin and outward-facing axis, which I'll use as the reference point for placing the sparkle just outside the eye's surface.

Positioning that tiny sparkle precisely is tricky — I want it offset toward the front and upper side of the eye along the surface, so I'm working out a small blended direction vector combining outward, up, and forward components scaled down to roughly the eye's radius so it sits right at the sphere's edge.

Now I'm placing the ear joints near the top of the skull, giving them exaggerated length for that alert fennec-kit look, and working out tilt and splay angles so each ear's extrude direction and outward normal face correctly for the left and right sides.

This orientation gives the ears a slight outward tilt at the top, which looks natural for alert fennec-style ears. The front face (facing the viewer) should be the pale peach lining, while the back shows the sandy fennec coloring, so I'll set up the paint function to check the face normal's z-component and apply peach gradient when it's positive.

For the gradient itself, I want a satin sheen effect transitioning from cream at the base to peach near the tip, using the surface coordinate's y-value to drive a smoothstep blend between the two colors.

Now I'm working out the leg chains for the fox kit—shoulder to knee to wrist to paw—placing each joint with specific coordinates so the paws rest naturally on the dune surface, with thin limbs and slightly oversized paw ellipsoids whose lowest points sink into the ground.

I'm settling on joint naming conventions for each limb chain: front legs as shoulder/elbow/wrist, hind legs as hip/knee/hock, distinguishing left and right with FL/BL style suffixes that satisfy the naming pattern requirements.

I'm deciding to build legs, tail, and neck using the chain API with explicit joint name lists and a parent reference to the torso, rather than constructing them manually through individual joints and sweeps.

For the leg chains, I'm mapping shoulder, knee, and wrist points to named joints (shoulderL/elbowL/wristL) so the elbow joint correctly drives bending of the lower leg segment, then sweeping a tube over the chain with a radius function that tapers from thicker thighs to thinner wrists for a fox-kit look.

For the paw, I'm attaching an ellipsoid sphere to the wrist joint, scaling it non-uniformly to create an oversized paw shape, and nudging its position slightly forward and down from the wrist so it reads as a touch oversized — considering cream/gold coloring to match a fennec-style coat.

Rather than adding separate toe spheres, I'll keep the paw as a single simplified ellipsoid for a stylized low-poly look, colored cream against sandy-gold legs. For overall body coloring, I'm planning a countershading approach — golden sand on the back where normals point up, cream on the belly and cheeks where they point down — using a reusable countershade paint function applied across body parts.

I'm reasoning through the normal-based blending (sides of the torso where normal.y is near zero will mix toward a 50/50 gradient), which actually matches the intended look of cream fading into sandy gold along the back. I also need to keep in mind that all these painted sweeps get baked into one shared texture atlas, so with many body parts the chart count and packing density could get tight.

For the chart count on tube-like shapes, I'm estimating roughly six charts per tube since triangles group by facing direction, which should keep packing manageable given the overall body surface area and the 1024px sheet size.

For the legs, I'm sticking with the same fur countershade paint on the main limb with cream for the paws, skipping dark socks for simplicity. For the hind legs, I'm mapping out the joint chain—hip, knee, hock—using a digitigrade bend (knee forward, hock angled back) and treating it as a two-segment polyline for the leg geometry.

For the front legs, I'm placing shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints in a straighter line with a slight forward angle, keeping coordinates consistent with where limbs attach to the body. I'm also checking paw placement against dune height at that radius, finding that the paws end up mostly sunk into the sand surface given the terrain height calculation there.

Realizing the paws are buried, I'm adjusting the dune profile to be flatter near the top with a defined height curve by radius, aiming to set a flat-ish crest around 0.085 height so the paws sit visibly on the surface rather than disappearing into it.

Now I'm rebuilding the entire skeleton with the ground reference raised to this new 0.085 top level — shifting shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw heights so each limb segment stacks correctly and the paw bottoms just touch the dune surface, then starting to work out torso and hip placement above that.

I'm placing the torso joints (hips, waist, chest, neck base, head) and front leg chain (shoulder→elbow→wrist) with specific coordinates, then working through the hind leg's digitigrade bend — hip forward to knee, back to hock, then forward again to the foot — mirroring the joint positions for the opposite side.

Now I'm setting up the neck as its own chain of three joints (neckA, neckB, head), where the tip joint doubles as the head's attachment point, oriented using the tangent direction at the end of the path. I'm reasoning that the rig's exact joint naming doesn't matter much functionally, just that the chain connects properly to the chest as its parent.

For the tail, I'm sketching a curved path sweeping backward and slightly downward from the rump using catmull-rom through a few points, checking that the number of names matches the span count. I'm planning a fluffy taper where the radius bulges in the middle and narrows toward a rounded tip, with a dark smudge accent near the end.

Writing paint blend logic...

For the tail tip, I want a soft black smudge that fades in using smoothstep against the source t-coordinate, with a touch of noise to make the edge ragged rather than a hard line. For the nose, I'm thinking a small dark sphere geometry anchored at the snout tip bone, or alternatively painting it directly onto the loft surface.

I'm also planning to give the creature a proper jaw joint so the mouth can articulate — a separate lower jaw sweep attached to its own jaw bone, running from the chin tip back along the underside, distinct from the upper head loft.

I still need to decide which chains should carry rig roles like head, neck, spine, leg, and tail for the rig system. For the collar, I'm thinking of building it as a closed sweep ring around the neck base, roughly matching the neck's thickness, to attach the brass bell to later.

Rather than fight the frame orientation, I'll just go with a small circular section for the band so it looks like a simple rope ring, and fake the woven texture using a paint function that creates a diagonal stripe pattern based on position along the loop and angle around the cross-section.

Now I'm thinking about how to position the collar itself — it needs to sit rigidly near the neck base, so I'll attach it as a bone-weighted ring around the neck joint, computing the circle's center and orientation from the neck's direction vector so the collar plane sits perpendicular to the neck.

Then I work out the bell's placement, hanging it at the front-bottom of the collar ring by picking the angle on the circle that points downward and forward.

I'm considering a small brass sphere for the bell shape, debating whether to add a tiny dark slit or loop detail, and ultimately decide to shape it as a lathed bell profile for a cleaner cup-like form.

Defining lathe points...

Negative y values should be fine for the lathe profile since only x is constrained to be non-negative. Now I need to work out where the bell actually attaches—computing the collar center point along the neck chain and figuring out how its radius compares to the torso's width at that height, so the collar sits naturally against the body rather than floating or clipping through it.

I'm computing the neck direction vector and its cross product with the X axis to get the vertical offset for the collar's front-bottom point, then generating the ring of collar points via a closed Catmull-Rom curve that gets swept into a tube for the woven collar geometry, making sure the closed-path seam and bone-weighting logic handle it correctly.

I'm reconsidering collar section shape—circle vs box—and sides count, then adjusting the collar's centerline radius so the tube sits closer to the neck surface instead of floating above it.

Working out where the collar sits along the neck chain's parametrized path, and then placing the bell pendant just below and in front of the collar, computing its center position relative to the chest/throat area.

I'm settling the overall coordinate layout: placing the dune centered near the origin with a flattened radius, letting the fox's body and tail extend across and slightly above its slope, and working out a radius profile for the dune's lathe cross-section with smoothed edges.

I decide against corner smoothing for the dune shape since it isn't needed, and consider that the default lathe segment count will give a slightly polygonal, low-poly dome look, which actually fits the intended style.

Now I'm working out the dune color scheme—sandy gold on top transitioning to dusky mauve on the sides using a level-based countershade—and calculating paw placement to make sure the fox's feet sit properly against the dune's curved surface. I'm computing paw center coordinates from the wrist and hock joints, checking that the dune's radial height at each paw's position roughly matches where I want the paws to rest, accepting a small amount of sinking into the surface at some points.

Now I'm structuring the torso skeleton, defining a hip joint as root and a spine chain running through waist and chest points, but I run into a naming collision issue—since the chain's first joint lands at the same position as the hip, I need to rework how I name the spine joints to avoid duplicating the hips joint.

So the root chain actually needs a joint created first since boneFor fails with no existing joints, meaning I need a separate "pelvis" root joint, then have the spine chain start at the waist point rather than hips, giving one span from waist to chest with proper parent linkage to pelvis.

I think I've settled on a clI like putting a "root" joint at ground level (0,0,0) to carry the dune geometry, with "hips" as its child at the pelvis position carrying the fox body chain. This gives a clean structure: root (ground, dune-weighted) → hips (pelvis) → spine chain, avoiding duplicate naming issues while keeping the hierarchy sensible.

Now I'm defining the spine chain itself, running from hips up through waist to chest, parented to root, then sweeping a tapered torso body along it with radius varying slightly by position to give a rounder chest and narrower waist, fox-style.

For the hind legs, I'm starting a new chain anchored at the hip socket point, planning to hang it down from the hips joint.

The thigh will taper from a chunky 0.028 radius at the hip down to 0.013 at the hock, giving it that haunch-heavy fennec look. For parent references, I'm confirming that joint names can just be passed as strings and resolved through the context lookup, which simplifies wiring up the chains—so I'll use string names consistently for all parent and joint references going forward, including the front legs attaching at the chest.

For symmetry I'll write a single parameterized function that handles left/right sides by flipping the x-coordinate sign, reusing it for both legs and ears, and continue defining the neck chain running from the chest tip up through two intermediate joints to the head.

I'm computing the collar ring's position and orientation along the neck by finding the tangent direction at a point partway along the first neck segment, then deriving perpendicular vectors to place the ring points around that circle.

For the bell pendant, I'm checking where it would sit relative to the collar and torso — finding it initially sinks into the chest's front bulge, so I shift it further forward and down to hang properly in front of the neck below the collar.

Now I'm laying out the head geometry as a sequence of loft stations from the back of the skull through cranium, cheek, muzzle, snout, to the nose tip, each with its own width and height, tilting the axis slightly upward toward the nose.

I'm verifying the loft and sweep code binds the head mesh rigidly to the head joint, confirming the Catmull-Rom spline through the stations and the skinning weights are set up correctly.

For coloring I'm planning a countershade paint with gold on top of the head and cream underneath for the muzzle and cheeks, giving the fennec its pale-faced look. I'm also locating the eye positions by finding the nearest surface points near the skull's narrowing region, sizing them as fairly large dark spheres to match the big-eyed fennec look, with a dark brown-black color and a white sparkle highlight.

Now I'm working out ear placement — figuring out where the base attaches on top of the head and how tall the ears should extend, landing on proportions that read as appropriately oversized. I'm deciding to give each ear its own joint parented to the head rather than just rigidly extruding them, so they can be rigged and posed independently, with the joint orientation pointing upward along the ear's growth direction.

I'm sketching the ear outline shape with a rounded leaf-like silhouette, picking smoothing and bevel values for softness, then setting up a paint function that shades the inner face peachy and the outer face a deeper sand tone based on surface normal direction. I'm also reasoning through the module's export structure to make sure the `mix` helper I need for blending colors is the right one being pulled in.

Then I move to facial details — placing a small dark nose at the snout tip with a slight flattening, and designing a lower jaw as its own joint and loft so the mouth can open, working through station widths and heights to make sure it nests under the upper muzzle without poking through. I consider adding cheek fluff but decide to keep the design lean.

Next I plan the tail as a joint chain running from the hips through a curved path to a tapered, fluffy tip, defining a radius function that bulges in the middle and narrows at both ends, with a darker tip color. Finally, I think about scattering small pebble geometries across the dune surface for texture, choosing a keep-out zone around the fox so pebbles don't spawn under its paws, and settling on a couple of muted colors for them while keeping total part count in mind.

I then work out the full color palette for the piece — gold and cream fur tones, peach ear interiors, dark eyes and nose, brass and leather collar colors, and a two-tone sandy-mauve dune — and start composing paint functions: a mottled gold-to-cream countershaded fur for the body, a woven checker pattern for the leather collar using cell-based parity logic, a countershaded sand-to-mauve gradient for the dune, and a custom tail paint that blends the body fur color into a noisy black smudge near the tip using a nested resolve call.

Writing paint functions...

With the palette and shading logic settled, I move into listing every import I'll need from the three.js and builder SDKs, then start double-checking each builder method's call signature — joints, chains, sweeps, lofts, parts, sticks, extrudes, lathes, and surfaces — to make sure arguments like color, bone, position, and direction are all correctly typed and that paint instances resolve properly as fill colors rather than being mistaken for functions.

I then catch a subtle bug in my ear orientation math: if I set the extrude's x-axis straight along world X, the builder will automatically orthogonalize it against my intended lean direction and cancel out the tilt I wanted. So I'm recalculating the x and y basis vectors for each ear so that the outward lean survives the orthogonalization, working out the correct tilted x vector for the left ear before mirroring it for the right.

I'm then placing the ear joints and double-checking that the ear base sits just barely embedded into the skull surface using the dome's ellipse equation, so the ears look rooted rather than floating; I settle on final base coordinates and a corresponding joint with an outward-up-forward direction.

Next I work out paw placement and proportions — sizing them as flattened ellipsoid spheres roughly 1.3x oversized relative to the leg thickness, computing exact heights so they land flush against the dune's sloped surface using the dune's radial height profile, and mirroring the math for both front and hind paws. I also sketch in a few small sphere "toe" bumps on each paw for readability.

I settle on tapering radius functions for the front and hind leg sweeps and the neck, reusing the countershaded fur paint, and note that the neck tube stays mostly hidden inside the chest geometry so its exact radius isn't too sensitive.

I debate adding small cheek tufts as cone-shaped spikes pointing outward from the skull surface for extra fluffy detail, weighing whether they'd look charming or messy, and tentatively plan a couple per side using surface-hit points and outward-facing directions, while deciding I can cut them later if the complexity budget gets tight.

Finally I plan scattering small pebble details across the dune surface, filtering out any sample points on the flat bottom disc or too close to the fox's footprint so they only land on the sloped faces, using a handful of dusky stone colors and small dodecahedron shapes stuck to the surface with normal-aligned orientation.

I then sanity-check overall proportions — tallying ear height, nose-to-tail length, and shoulder height against a real fennec kit's typical measurements, and conclude the body reads as a stylized big-headed kit rather than strictly anatomical, which feels like an acceptable creative choice given the whimsical brief rather than something to over-correct.

I begin drafting the actual module: imports from the builder library, a color palette (gold, cream, peach, ink, brass, dune tones), and paint definitions using mottle and countershade for the fur and dune texture, plus procedural paints for the ear coloring (peach gradient with sandy backs), the tail (coat color fading to an ink tip with noisy blending), a woven-looking two-tone leather paint for the collar using a checkered surface-coordinate pattern, and simple solid colors for eyes and nose.

I start building the model function: creating the builder, placing a root joint, and lathing the dune's cross-section profile into a rotated solid using the earlier height values, then constructing the spine as a three-point chain from hips through waist to chest with named joints for rigging.

Writing leg sweeps...

I add the nose as a small embedded sphere stretched wider than tall for a fox-like shape, then introduce a jaw joint hinged off the head, and loft a cream lower jaw running from near the hinge down to a tapered chin tip, checking that it nests just below the upper skull's profile so a thin mouth-line gap peeks through.

I weigh whether to add small cheek fluff tufts using spike-based cones, but decide the composition is already rich enough with the dune, ears, collar, bell, tail tip, sparkling eyes, and paws, so I skip the tufts to keep things clean.

Writing ear extrude code...

I work out the collar by generating a ring of points around the neck axis using two perpendicular directions to define its tilt, then sweep that closed loop into a thin tube rigidly bound to the neck's base joint, confirming the orientation and spacing match the neck's slope.
